messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
parts:
Hi all,

I have a relatively simple Poisson regression problem with n=700, and about 20 regressors (so around 20 regression coefficients).

The adaptation period is, I think, unexpectedly slow, at around one sample per few seconds..

If I start with inits=0,  the chain basically doesn't move for the first few hundred iterations, then moves thereafter.  If I start with init = the parameters from the mode found by the optimiser, the rate of sampling is relatively constant.

After looking at the sampler parameters, max_treedepth is hit the whole way through the first hundreds of iterations.  Increasing max_treedepth up to 12 in accordance with the suggestion in the manual just makes the sampling take a lot longer (tree depth keeps hitting 12).

After adaptation for n=500 iterations (250 warmup and 250 sampling), the effective sample sizes for the parameters are quite high however - often near 250.

I suspect that the problem may be due to some of my regressors.  Groups of regressors unavoidably define a simplex (ie the sum of each of the regressors in a particular group is one).  In fact, I omit one of the regressors from the simplex due to the linear dependence (eg if regressors 1 through 8 define a simplex, then I only use 1 through 7 in the model in order to avoid the degeneracy).  For example, one of my regressors is the percentage of people in a particular age group, eg ages 0-17, 18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, and 80+.  In this context I omit the "80+" group to avoid the total degeneracy.

In order to mitigate the potential degeneracy issue and to implement shrinkage, I have put a hierarchical prior on each of the simplex-like groups of regressors with a zero mean (eg age[i] ~ normal(0, sig_age)  in the example above), and I have put a vaguely informative prior on sig_age.

There are a number of possible other causes:
  • Scale of regressors (and therefore potential scale of regression coefficients) does vary somewhat - by about 3 orders of magnitude
  • I have not used the Matt trick - but if I try removing the hierarchical priors (sig_age in the example above) the speed is not significantly affected, so perhaps this is not the cause
Things I have tried:
  • I have vectorised all the sampling statements, so this isn't the issue.
  • I have tried using a dense mass matrix, and this doesn't seem to make any significant difference.

My question is:  has anyone encountered behaviour like this, and do you have any solutions?  I cannot avoid the use of simplex regressors in this case, but in some cases could amalgamate the groups (but do not wish to do so if I can avoid it).

I appreciate that maybe I just have to live with the slow sampling - perhaps Stan is behaving as expected.  

Thoughts appreciated about where my efforts in optimising the model are best spent.

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
parts:
Sometimes fitting a more general model can be faster. I'd be surprised if
that were the case with the Poisson --- usually we have more trouble
estimating the overdispersion.

Scale variation of several orders of magnitude essentially introduces
stiffness into Stan's ODE solver --- it can't go too fast in the most
highly constrained dimension.

The problem is that it needs to learn which dimension that is during
warmup, which would explain why things are OK after warmup. If there's a
way you could rescale, that'd probably help a lot.

You can take a look at the scaling parameters after the run to see what
warmup did.

Tree depth of 10 is 1024 log probability and gradient evals per iteration,
and depth 12 is 4 times that many. That's the main reason it's going to
be slow.

- Bob

To unask the last question, the lgamma function is used for
the Poisson, but it's only calculated if you call poisson_log(...)
as a function. If you use sampling notation, it will be a constant
and be dropped.

When log factorials are needed, we calculate them using the lgamma function
from Boost:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_59_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/sf_gamma/lgamma.html

and digamma and trigamma for derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
parts:
I don't know how strict that truncation is (seems to be Poisson and
overdispersed and zero-inflated Poisson week), but rather than

y[n] ~ poisson(alpha[n]) T[1,];

you could use

(y[n] - 1) ~ poisson(alpha[n]);

Of course, the interpretation of alpha[n] is slightly different.

Alternatively, you can do the simple case of the Poisson by realizing
that the relevant CDF (1 - poisson_cdf(1, alpha[n])) can be coded
as (1 - exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n])). Because you're going to need
that on the log scale, and it's a common operation, we have it built in
as

log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]);

So you could code the whole model as

y ~ poisson(alpha);
for (n in 1:N)
increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]));

Considerably uglier. Now if the alpha[n] were all the same, it
could be made much more efficient. As is, allowing the vectorization
now in the Poisson sampling statement shouldn't be too bad.

- Bob

Shouldn't this be

y ~ poisson(alpha);
for(i in 1:n){
    increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-alpha[i]));

According to p109 of the manual, the PDF should be
p(y | lambda) = Poisson(y | lambda) / (1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
so log p = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - exp(-lambda)
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log1m_exp(-lambda)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
parts:
Just to provide a further update on my general problem:

  • I have not been able to materially speed up the model (iterations per second) through simply recoding the Poisson calculation
  • I continued to struggle with convergence issues, until I standardised every regressor to have mean zero and standard deviation 1.  This has made a massive improvement to the model, I suspect by reducing posterior correlations (I have interaction terms as well, which behave oddly unless standardised).  I had some concerns about this given the simplex-like nature of blocks of my regressors, but in fact this seems to be fine.
  • I have had to use adapt_delta = 0.9 in order to minimise the number of divergent transitions
  • I have increased max_treedepth to 11, but still hit up against the max_treedepth quite often.

Yes, the parameter correlations are very high given the simplex constraint.  I have a Gaussian shrinkage prior on every parameter to try to deal with the problem, so the prior is nominally proper, but appreciate that it can take a long time to explore.
